title: Physics-Informed One-Step Generation on Long-short Flow Maps

paper.title: Physics-Informed One-Step Generation on Long-short Flow Maps
paper.abstract:
Abstract We propose Physics-Informed Long-Short Flow Maps with Direct Guidance (PI-LSFM), a one-step generative method for producing data-aligned and physically valid samples.
Existing one-step physics-informed generative models must jointly control data fidelity and physical constraints without the iterative correction of multi-step samplers, making it difficult to coordinate indirect surrogate supervision with strong physics enforcement.
PI-LSFM addresses this challenge by decomposing generation into a long flow map for global transport and a near-terminal short flow map, where closed-form data and physics potentials provide directly computable guidance targets instead of indirect regression surrogates.
The short map guides the long map during training, yielding a single one-step generator that requires neither staged distillation nor inference-time correction.
Across Darcy flow, Kolmogorov flow, dynamic stall, and topology optimization, PI-LSFM achieves a favorable trade-off among distributional fidelity, physical residuals, and inference efficiency while using only one function evaluation at inference.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Many problems in scientific machine learning are inherently distributional: under uncertain boundary conditions, perturbed parameters, incomplete observations, or intrinsic stochasticity, one seeks not a single deterministic solution, but a distribution of physically feasible ones. This makes generative modeling a natural framework for physical systems, as it can capture high-dimensional solution distributions while incorporating PDEs, conservation laws, and other physical constraints. Recent works have therefore introduced physics-informed diffusion and related generative frameworks to produce samples that are both statistically plausible and physically valid Shu et al. (2023) ; Huang et al. (2024) ; Jacobsen et al. (2025) . However, these methods typically rely on iterative multi-step generation and are often slow for practical use, which naturally motivates fast and ideally one-step physics-informed generation. The main difficulty, however, is not merely that one-step generation is harder to train, but that existing physics-informed diffusion methods rely on indirect supervision for both data and physics. On the data side, flow matching learns the data distribution through the surrogate regression objective ℒ data = 𝔼 ⁡ [ | u t θ ​ ( x t ) − u t ​ ( x t | x 1 ) | 2 ] \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{data}}=\mathbb{E}[|u_{t}^{\theta}(x_{t})-u_{t}(x_{t}|x_{1})|^{2}] , where the model is supervised by the conditional velocity u t ​ ( x t | x 1 ) u_{t}(x_{t}|x_{1}) because the true marginal velocity u t ​ ( x t ) u_{t}(x_{t}) is unavailable. On the physics side, directly applying a nonlinear residual to intermediate states causes a Jensen-type mismatch Bastek et al. (2024) ; existing methods therefore impose the residual on a reconstructed endpoint, ℒ phys = 𝔼 ⁡ [ | ℛ ⁡ ( x ^ 1 ​ ( x t ) ) | 2 ] \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{phys}}=\mathbb{E}[|\mathcal{R}(\hat{x}_{1}(x_{t}))|^{2}] , and use it to supervise intermediate states indirectly. This double indirectness makes distributional and physical objectives difficult to coordinate Baldan et al. (2026) . The issue is amplified in one-step methods such as MeanFlow Geng et al. (2025) and ShortCut Frans et al. (2025) . A long-range flow map ψ t → r \psi_{t\to r} is difficult to learn and, unlike an instantaneous velocity, lacks a consistent data-conditioned counterpart ψ t → r ( ⋅ | x 1 ) \psi_{t\to r}(\cdot|x_{1}) for surrogate supervision Li et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2026) . Moreover, one-step sampling removes the iterative correction available in multi-step methods Bastek et al. (2024) , requiring stronger physics enforcement during training. Thus, one-step physics-informed generation must couple a harder indirect distribution objective with a stronger physics objective, making training fragile. Even in endpoint-prediction methods such as sCM Lu & Song (2024) , where the residual can be applied directly to ψ t → 1 ​ ( x t ) \psi_{t\to 1}(x_{t}) , the data objective remains indirect. Chang et al. (2026) show that coupling strong physics constraints with indirect distribution objectives can lead to trivial solutions, severe mode collapse, and the need for two-stage distillation. Figure 1: PI-LSFM enables physics-informed one-step generation from scratch via long-short flow-map direct guidance, achieving multi-step-level performance on unconditional generation, conditional generation, and inverse design without increasing batch size or training steps, and without extra inference-time parameters or iterative correction. In this work, we study physics-informed one-step generation in flow-map-based frameworks and aim to enable stable training from scratch through direct data-distribution and physics-constraint objectives. This is difficult in existing methods: closed-form flow-matching solutions are typically too inefficient for practical training Bertrand et al. (2025) , while directly imposing physical constraints at intermediate states leads to Jensen’s gap. Our key observation is that both objectives can be imposed directly in the near-terminal data neighborhood, where they provide effective and correct guidance for learning the full flow map. This motivates a long-short flow-map approach, which decomposes one-step generation into a long flow map for global evolution and a near-terminal short flow map driven by computable closed-form solutions and physics potentials. As Δ ​ t → 0 \Delta t\to 0 , the short flow map shrinks away while providing direct data-distribution and physics-constraint guidance for learning the long flow map. This yields Long-Short Flow Maps with Direct Guidance (PI-LSFM), where data learning and physical validity are guided by near-terminal, directly computable targets rather than conditional-regression surrogates or reconstructed terminal states. A detailed discussion of related work is provided in Appendix A . Our contributions: (1) We propose a long-short flow-map framework that addresses indirect-objective instability by modeling the short flow map as dynamics jointly driven by data and physics potentials, enabling direct guidance from distributional and physical constraints for one-step generation. (2) We study the numerical design and computation of the short flow map, leading to a stable and efficient training procedure with improved distributional fidelity and physical consistency. (3) We validate PI-LSFM on unconditional generation, conditional generation, and topology optimization, where it consistently achieves strong performance on practical physics-informed generation tasks.

In subsection 4.1 , we compare different encoder choices, including several physics foundation models. The encoder is used only to stabilize the kernel-weighted estimation of the data guidance target in high-dimensional field spaces. Without the encoder, Darcy flow still achieves reasonable physical residuals and only slightly poorer distribution matching (RE=0.044, WD ⋅ 10 2 \cdot 10^{2} = 0.446, and JS ⋅ 10 1 \cdot 10^{1} = 0.889), but becomes more prone to training collapse, as illustrated in Figure 11 . We use it only for the weakly conditioned Darcy and Kolmogorov flow benchmarks (Sections 4.1 and 4.2 ), while dynamic stall (Section 4.2 ) and topology optimization (Section 4.3 ) are trained directly without any encoder. Although MAE roughly doubles the per-step training time (0.271s vs. 0.132s without an encoder), PI-LSFM uses about one third of the training steps of Baldan et al. (2026) , largely offsetting this overhead. Unlike latent-based generation, PI-LSFM still generates ψ 0 → 1 θ ​ ( x 0 ) \psi_{0\to 1}^{\theta}(x_{0}) in the original space and computes only the loss in feature space; see subsection C.2 and Figure 5 .

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We choose the four benchmarks to progressively evaluate unconditional generation, conditional generalization, coupled multi-field physical constraints, and physics-constrained inverse design. We use the U-Net architecture of Bastek et al. (2024) without architecture-specific optimization, and match parameter counts whenever possible. For fair comparison, we report NFE and wall-clock inference time when available, using standard sampling settings or reported numbers for multi-step baselines. Since multi-step samplers benefit from iterative refinement, we target a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off rather than uniformly dominating every metric. All experiments use an NVIDIA A100 GPU. Our main benchmark results are obtained from single training runs with the fixed seed 42 and no seed selection. Appendix G.2 , Table 17 reports a three-seed, 100K-step Darcy stability check.

sections.heading: 4.1 Darcy Flow and Design Studies
sections.text: Darcy flow is a two-dimensional steady-state porous-media benchmark on 64 × 64 64\times 64 pressure p p and permeability K K fields, with 10k training and 1k validation samples. Following Baldan et al. (2026) , we enforce the Darcy residual ℛ pde = ∇ ⋅ ( K ∇ p ) + f = 0 \mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{pde}}=\nabla\cdot(K\nabla p)+f=0 together with the boundary-condition loss, and evaluate physical validity and distributional fidelity using residual error (RE), Wasserstein distance (WD), and Jensen–Shannon divergence (JS) of pressure field. This is an unconditional generation task, and lower values indicate better performance. On Darcy flow, we compare with multi-step baselines PBFM Baldan et al. (2026) , FM-OT Lipman et al. (2023) , CoCoGen Jacobsen et al. (2025) , PIDM Bastek et al. (2024) , DiffusionPDE Huang et al. (2024) , D-Flow Ben-Hamu et al. (2024) , and ECI Cheng et al. (2024) , using reported numbers from Baldan et al. (2026) , as well as our one-step flow-map baselines built on sCM-PINN Chang et al. (2026) . As shown in Figure 3(d) and 4(a) , our method significantly outperforms other one-step methods, matches strong multi-step baselines, and lies on the best Pareto front, while using fewer training steps with the same batch size and roughly matched parameter count to the PBFM baseline. At inference, its one-step sampling yields substantial acceleration, including about a 5 × 5\times speedup over architecture-optimized PBFM under a standard backbone. Additional experimental details, including the training procedure, evaluation metrics, and qualitative visualizations, are given in subsection E.2 . To stabilize training, we adopt the feature-space stabilization strategy described in subsection 3.3 . We study different encoder choices, including a multi-resolution MAE trained on this dataset He et al. (2022) , the pretrained multi-resolution U-Net-based physics foundation model Poseidon Herde et al. (2024) , the transformer-based physics foundation model DPOT Hao et al. (2024) , and MPP McCabe et al. (2024) . The results show that MAE, Poseidon, and DPOT achieve comparable performance, with MAE providing the strongest overall results and the fastest training speed. We therefore use MAE as the encoder for Darcy and Kolmogorov flow (Sections 4.1 and 4.2 ). In Figure 3(c) and Figure 3(b) , we further compare different numerical schemes for the data term and the physics term, respectively, while fixing the other term to its best-performing choice. The results show that the second-order trapezoidal rule works best for the data term, while Forward Euler performs best for the physics term. A more complete design study and parameter study, including the λ ¯ \bar{\lambda} schedule, is provided in Appendix D . sections.heading: 4.2 Kolmogorov Flow and Dynamic Stall
sections.text: We evaluate conditional generation on two-dimensional incompressible Kolmogorov flow following Baldan et al. (2026) . The model is conditioned on the Reynolds number and evaluated on 16 unseen Reynolds numbers, testing generalization across turbulent flow regimes. Physical consistency is enforced through the incompressibility constraint ∇ ⋅ U = 0 \nabla\cdot U=0 . As shown in Table 3 , PI-LSFM achieves strong physical and distributional performance while requiring only a single function evaluation, compared with 20-step baselines. We report physical residual error (RE), distributional metrics (WD and JS), conditional-statistics errors (MMSE and SMSE), and inference efficiency (NFE and IT). Full dataset, metric, and implementation details are provided in Appendix E.3 . We further evaluate PI-LSFM on conditional generation for dynamic stall, a compressible-flow benchmark around a sinusoidally pitching NACA0012 airfoil following Baldan et al. (2026) . The model predicts six coupled aerodynamic and thermodynamic fields conditioned on four operating and motion parameters, and is evaluated on unseen configurations. Physical consistency is enforced through the ideal-gas relation and a temperature-dependent skin-friction constraint based on Sutherland’s law. As shown in Table 3 , PI-LSFM achieves competitive performance relative to multi-step baselines while requiring only one function evaluation. The evaluation follows the same distributional, statistical, and efficiency metrics as Kolmogorov flow. Full problem formulation, residual definitions, training details, and qualitative results are provided in Appendix E.4 .

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced Long-Short Flow Maps with Direct Guidance (PI-LSFM), a one-step physics-informed generative framework that decomposes the full flow map into a long-range map and a near-terminal short map. This decomposition converts indirect flow-map and physics-informed supervision into a directly computable near-terminal guidance target, enabling joint data and physics guidance. We studied numerical instantiations of the short-flow dynamics and their effects on stability and generation quality. Experiments on unconditional generation, conditional generation, and physics-constrained inverse design show that PI-LSFM achieves a favorable trade-off among stability, distributional fidelity, physical consistency, and inference efficiency, matching strong multi-step baselines while preserving one-step efficiency without distillation. Our framework has several limitations. Similar to prior physics-informed generative methods Baldan et al. (2026) ; Bastek et al. (2024) , PI-LSFM enforces physical constraints only during training, leaving inference-time constraint enforcement to future work. It would be interesting to combine PI-LSFM with inference-time constraint methods Cheng et al. (2024) ; Chang et al. (2026) . We study only a limited set of numerical schemes for the data and physics terms; broader numerical families may further improve stability and performance. Scaling to larger models, datasets, and more complex physics tasks is another important direction.

sections.heading: Physics-informed generation.
sections.text: Physics-informed generative methods can be broadly divided into training-time and inference-time approaches. Training-time methods incorporate physical constraints directly into the learning objective. For example, physics-informed diffusion models Bastek et al. (2024) ; Shu et al. (2023) add PDE residuals or boundary losses during training, while CoCoGen Jacobsen et al. (2025) and DiffusionPDE Huang et al. (2024) study physically consistent generation and PDE-conditioned modeling. FunDiff Wang et al. (2025) instead formulates physics-informed generative modeling over function spaces. Inference-time methods guide or correct samples during generation. D-Flow Ben-Hamu et al. (2024) differentiates through the generative flow for controlled generation, while hard-constrained and gradient-free methods Utkarsh et al. (2025) ; Cheng et al. (2024) enforce constraints during sampling without fully retraining the generator. Physics-informed distillation (PIDDM) Zhang & Zou (2025) follows a teacher-based route, distilling a pretrained diffusion model into a one-step generator for PDE-constrained generation. PI-LSFM instead trains a one-step generator from scratch using joint data and physics guidance, without a pretrained generative teacher. Most closely related to our work, Physics vs Distributions Baldan et al. (2026) highlights the trade-off between distribution matching and physical validity, and proposes a Pareto-optimal flow-matching framework with physics constraints. Physics-informed consistency models Chang et al. (2026) , building on continuous-time consistency models Lu & Song (2024) , aim to stabilize one-step physics-informed generation through structure-preserving training. In contrast, our long-short flow-map direct guidance provides a direct one-step training objective that better balances distributional fidelity and physical validity, without requiring iterative inference-time correction.

sections.heading: One-step generation.
sections.text: Early one-step generative models were mainly developed through distillation or adversarial training. For example, distribution matching distillation Yin et al. (2024) compresses multi-step diffusion sampling into a single-step generator, while GAN-based methods Heusel et al. (2017) directly learn one-step mappings with adversarial objectives. More recently, increasing attention has been given to training one-step generators from scratch without relying on a pretrained teacher. A prominent direction formulates one-step generation as learning a flow map from noise to data Boffi et al. (2025) . Representative methods include consistency models Song et al. (2023) ; Lu & Song (2024) ; Geng et al. (2024) , shortcut models Frans et al. (2025) , mean-flow methods Geng et al. (2025) , and extensions such as functional mean flow Li et al. (2025) . More recently, drifting models Deng et al. (2026) revisit one-step generation from a distribution-matching perspective, improving the stability and scalability of training-from-scratch one-step generators and concurrent work Li & Zhu (2026) provides a long-short flow-map interpretation of drifting models. Our work instead studies physics-informed one-step generation, where the central challenge is to balance data-distribution fidelity and physical constraint satisfaction within a single flow map. We analyze this interaction through a potential-based formulation, which avoids the terminal-time singularity of velocity-based formulations at t = 1 t=1 , and propose a long-short flow-map framework with direct guidance for joint control of distributional and physical objectives. PI-LSFM starts from a long-short flow-map decomposition of physics-informed one-step generation, providing a unified framework for analyzing and constructing direct guidance from both the data distribution and physical constraints. The near-terminal short flow is jointly driven by data and physics potentials, while different numerical discretizations induce explicit, implicit, and projection-based update rules within the same construction. This framework also clarifies its connection to drifting models Deng et al. (2026) : under a particular raw-space specialization, the data-side correction recovers a drifting-style update. PI-LSFM extends beyond this special case by jointly deriving physics guidance, systematically studying alternative data and physics discretizations, and supporting feature-space guidance for high-dimensional physical fields. The matched one-step comparisons and numerical studies evaluate these components and their interaction in physics-informed generation.

sections.heading: Physics foundation models.
sections.text: Self-supervised learning has recently enabled foundation models for scientific systems. Inspired by vision methods such as masked autoencoders (MAE) He et al. (2022) , PDE foundation models aim to learn transferable spatiotemporal representations across equations, parameters, and conditions. Representative examples include Poseidon Herde et al. (2024) , which uses multiscale operator learning for fluid-dynamics pretraining; DPOT Hao et al. (2024) , which learns autoregressive denoising operators with a transformer backbone; and MPP McCabe et al. (2024) , which pretrains surrogate models across multiple physical systems. PROSE-FD Liu et al. (2024) incorporates multimodal PDE descriptions and numerical fields, while MORPH Rautela et al. (2025) and SPUS Siddik et al. (2025) further address heterogeneous modalities, resolutions, and parameter efficiency. Unlike these works, we use physics foundation models only as feature encoders to stabilize our kernel-based training objective, while generation remains in the original physical field space.

sections.heading: D.1 Physics Term Numerical Integration Study
sections.text: We next study the impact of different numerical discretizations in Table 2 for the physics term. Specifically, we compare Forward Euler, Backward Euler, and Backward Euler(limit), while fixing the data term to its best-performing configuration, namely the trapezoidal rule. In the experiments, we evaluate four constant values of the coefficient λ ¯ \bar{\lambda} from 0.1 0.1 to 3.0 3.0 , which controls the relative strength between the data term and the physics term. For each numerical scheme, we plot the trends of RE, WD, and JS as λ ¯ \bar{\lambda} varies, as shown in 6(a) , 6(d) and 6(g) . Unlike Forward Euler, Backward Euler does not exhibit a simple smooth trend. In particular, as shown in 6(d) , WD and JS increase sharply when λ ¯ \bar{\lambda} changes from 0.3 0.3 to 0.1 0.1 . To address this sensitivity, we additionally consider three scheduling strategies for λ ¯ \bar{\lambda} : piecewise, linear, and quadratic schedules. Let s s denote the training step, and let s warm s_{\mathrm{warm}} and s ramp s_{\mathrm{ramp}} denote the end of the warm-up stage and ramping stage, respectively. The piecewise schedule is defined as λ ¯ ​ ( s ) = { 0.1 , s < s warm , 1.0 , s warm ≤ s < s ramp , 3.0 , s ≥ s ramp . \bar{\lambda}(s)=\begin{cases}0.1,&s<s_{\mathrm{warm}},\\ 1.0,&s_{\mathrm{warm}}\leq s<s_{\mathrm{ramp}},\\ 3.0,&s\geq s_{\mathrm{ramp}}.\end{cases} with s ramp = 200 ​ k s_{\mathrm{ramp}}=200k and s warm = 50 ​ k {\color[rgb]{0,0,0}s_{\mathrm{warm}}}=50k . To better compare the trade-off between the data term and the physics term under different constant and scheduled choices of λ ¯ \bar{\lambda} , we also plot RE-WD and RE-JS scatter plots. These plots allow us to select the best configuration for each numerical scheme. We observe that Forward Euler consistently achieves better trade-offs across RE, WD, and JS compared with the two implicit variants. We then select the best-performing λ ¯ \bar{\lambda} for each method and report the corresponding RE, WD, and JS in Figure 3(b) . The selected configurations are λ ¯ = 3.0 \bar{\lambda}=3.0 for Forward Euler, the piecewise schedule for Backward Euler, and the piecewise schedule for Backward Euler (limit). All experiments use the same model architecture and training configuration as in subsection E.2 . We train each variant for 400K steps. sections.heading: D.2 Data Term Numerical Integration Study
sections.text: We next study the effect of different numerical schemes in Table 1 for the data term. Similar to the physics-term study, we compare Forward Euler, Backward Euler, and the trapezoidal rule, while fixing the physics term to its best-performing configuration, namely the Forward Euler method. In the experiments, we evaluate five values of the coefficient λ ¯ \bar{\lambda} from 0.3 0.3 to 10.0 10.0 , which controls the relative strength between the data term and the physics term. For each numerical scheme, we plot the trends of RE, WD, and JS as λ ¯ \bar{\lambda} varies, as shown in Figure 7 . The trapezoidal rule consistently yields smaller values across all three metrics compared with the two Euler schemes. We then select the best-performing λ ¯ {\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bar{\lambda}} for each method and report the corresponding RE, WD, and JS in Figure 3(c) . The selected values are λ ¯ = 3.0 {\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bar{\lambda}}=3.0 for Forward Euler, λ ¯ = 10.0 \bar{\lambda}=10.0 for Backward Euler, and λ ¯ = 3.0 \bar{\lambda}=3.0 for the trapezoidal rule. All experiments use the same model architecture and training configuration as in subsection E.2 . To reduce computational cost, we train each variant for 100K steps. In contrast to the physics term, we find that the second-order trapezoidal rule consistently achieves the best performance for the data term. This can be attributed to the kernel-based expectation in the data target, where a higher-order discretization provides a more accurate approximation of the near-terminal dynamics. (a) Forward Euler. (b) Backward Euler. (c) Trapezoidal rule. Figure 7: Effect of the coefficient λ ¯ \bar{\lambda} under different numerical discretizations.

sections.heading: D.3 Encoder Study
sections.text: We investigate the effect of different feature encoders used in the feature-space stabilization strategy described in subsection 3.3 . The corresponding training procedure is summarized in Figure 5 . We consider several representative encoder choices, including a multi-resolution MAE He et al. (2022) trained on the target dataset, the pretrained U-Net-based physics foundation model Poseidon Herde et al. (2024) , and the transformer-based physics foundation models DPOT Hao et al. (2024) and MPP McCabe et al. (2024) . For a fair comparison, we keep the encoder parameter counts approximately matched at around 30M parameters. For Poseidon, we use the basic variant, while for DPOT and MPP, we use their small variants to ensure comparable model sizes. The MAE encoder is implemented as a ResNet–U-Net architecture trained directly on the Darcy dataset (for Kolmogorov flow, we use the same architecture and training setup, only adapting the input and output channels). Each input consists of two channels, which are first patchified using 2 × 2 2\times 2 patches, resulting in an 8-channel representation on a 32 × 32 32\times 32 grid. The encoder follows a ResNet34-style He et al. (2016) design with Group Normalization, producing multi-resolution feature maps with channel widths 64,128,256 , 64,128,256, and 512 512 . The decoder adopts a U-Net structure with bilinear upsampling and skip connections to reconstruct the input. During training, we randomly mask 50% of the patches and optimize a mean-squared reconstruction loss on the masked regions. The model is trained with batch size 256 using AdamW, with an initial learning rate of 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} decayed to 1.25 × 10 − 4 1.25\times 10^{-4} , weight decay 0, and β = ( 0.9 , 0.999 ) \beta=(0.9,0.999) , together with an exponential moving average with decay 0.9995. The MAE is trained for 400K steps, after which it is frozen and used as the feature encoder. We keep the neural representation of the flow map and the training configuration the same as in subsection E.2 . To reduce computational cost, each encoder variant is trained for 100K steps within the PI-LSFM framework. In the experiments, we evaluate five constant values of the coefficient λ ¯ \bar{\lambda} from 0.1 0.1 to 10.0 10.0 , which controls the relative strength between the data term and the physics term. For each encoder, we plot the trends of RE, WD, and JS as λ ¯ \bar{\lambda} varies, as shown in Figure 8 . These plots allow us to select the best configuration for each encoder and compare different encoders under their respective best-performing settings. We then report the corresponding RE, WD, JS, and per-step training time in Figure 3(a) . The selected configurations use λ ¯ = 3.0 \bar{\lambda}=3.0 for MAE, λ ¯ = 1.0 \bar{\lambda}=1.0 for Poseidon, and λ ¯ = 10.0 \bar{\lambda}=10.0 for DPOT and MPP. We observe that all encoders improve the performance of our model, demonstrating the effectiveness and robustness of feature-space training. Among them, MAE, Poseidon, and DPOT achieve the strongest overall results. Since MAE provides the fastest training while maintaining strong performance, we use it as the default encoder in our subsequent experiments. Nevertheless, for settings where training a task-specific encoder is undesirable, pretrained encoders such as Poseidon and DPOT remain strong alternatives. To construct the feature space, we avoid directly flattening the full encoder feature maps, as this would lead to prohibitively high dimensionality. Instead, following Deng et al. (2026) , we aggregate the encoder outputs into a compact set of multi-scale statistics. For each feature map of size H i × W i × C i H_{i}\times W_{i}\times C_{i} , we retain location-wise features, global channel-wise mean and standard deviation, and channel-wise mean and standard deviation computed over spatial patches at multiple resolutions. This design preserves both local and global information while significantly reducing the dimensionality of the feature representation. In Figure 11 , we demonstrate the necessity of feature-space optimization: without a feature encoder, training fails, in contrast to the successful feature-space results in Figure 10 . (a) MAE. (b) Poseidon. (c) DPOT. (d) MPP. Figure 8: Effect of the coefficient λ ¯ \bar{\lambda} for different feature encoders. Each plot shows RE, WD, and JS as λ ¯ \bar{\lambda} varies.

sections.heading: Dataset
sections.text: To clearly demonstrate the advantage of our direct loss in jointly controlling the physics constraint and the data distribution, we consider a two-dimensional toy dataset for intuitive visualization. Specifically, we construct 𝒟 = { ( x i , y i ) } i = 1 n \mathcal{D}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} from a mixture of three Gaussian distributions whose centers are approximately located on the unit circle. The underlying physical constraint is ‖ ( x , y ) ‖ 2 = 1 \|(x,y)\|^{2}=1 . To simulate a realistic setting where data samples are influenced by both the data distribution and the physical constraint, we do not fully project the samples onto the circle. Instead, we introduce controlled deviations by interpolating between the original Gaussian samples and their projections x final = ( 1 − α ) ​ x raw + α ​ x proj x_{\mathrm{final}}=(1-\alpha)x_{\mathrm{raw}}+\alpha x_{\mathrm{proj}} , where α = 0.9 \alpha=0.9 in all experiments. This produces training samples that approximately satisfy the constraint while preserving the multimodal structure of the data. An example of this training dataset is shown in 9(a) , while the fully projected dataset in 9(b) serves as the desired physics-consistent distribution.

sections.heading: Training Details
sections.text: On this dataset, we compare our method with a single-stage consistency model (sCM Lu & Song (2024) ). For sCM, we use the standard consistency objective ℒ sCM = 𝔼 | [ | ∥ F θ ( x t 1 , t 1 ) − sg | ( F θ ( x t 2 , t 2 ) | ) | ∥ 2 | ] + λ ¯ 𝔼 | [ ∥ ℛ ( f θ ( x t , t ) | ) ∥ 2 ] \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sCM}}=\mathbb{E}|[|\|F_{\theta}(x_{t_{1}},t_{1})-\mathrm{sg}\!|(F_{\theta}(x_{t_{2}},t_{2})|)|\|^{2}|]+\bar{\lambda}\mathbb{E}|[\|\mathcal{R}\!(f_{\theta}(x_{t},t)|)\|^{2}] , where F θ F_{\theta} denotes the raw neural-network output and f θ f_{\theta} denotes the corresponding consistency output used for generation. ℛ ⁡ ( x , y ) = x 2 + y 2 − 1 \mathcal{R}(x,y)=x^{2}+y^{2}-1 is the physics residual for the circle constraint. Except for the training loss, our method and sCM use the same model architecture and optimization setup. We use a MLP network as the backbone. The network has 8 layers with hidden dimension 128 and sinusoidal time embeddings of dimension 32. Both methods are trained for 40K steps using AdamW with learning rate 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} , weight decay 0 0 , and β = ( 0.9 , 0.999 ) \beta=(0.9,0.999) . We use exponential moving average (EMA) with decay 0.9999 0.9999 .

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: We visualize the learned distributions in Figure 9 using a small batch size B = 3 B=3 , which highlights whether each method can simultaneously recover the multimodal distribution and satisfy the circle constraint. For sCM, we test multiple values of the physics weight λ \lambda for a fair comparison. As shown in Figures 9(d) – 9(i) , physics-informed consistency models struggle to balance the data distribution and the constraint: small λ \lambda leads to poor constraint satisfaction, while large λ \lambda causes the physics term to dominate and often results in mode collapse. In contrast, our method in 9(c) enforces the geometric constraint while preserving the three modes along the circle, demonstrating effective joint control of distributional fidelity and physical validity. sections.heading: Dataset and constraints.
sections.text: Kolmogorov flow is a standard benchmark for two-dimensional incompressible turbulence, where the dynamics are driven by a spatially periodic forcing. We follow the dataset construction in Baldan et al. (2026) , where velocity fields are defined on a 128 × 128 128\times 128 periodic domain and conditioned on the Reynolds number, which determines the flow regime. The data are generated using a spectral solver based on the vorticity–streamfunction formulation of the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations. Specifically, the vorticity field is evolved in time, and the velocity field U = ( u , v ) U=(u,v) is recovered from the stream function, while the pressure is obtained by solving a Poisson equation. The simulations are performed for Reynolds numbers in the range [ 100,500 ] [100,500] , with 32 distinct values used for training and 16 unseen values reserved for evaluation. For each Reynolds number, multiple trajectories are simulated from perturbed initial conditions, and snapshots are collected after the flow reaches a statistically steady regime, resulting in 1024 1024 samples per condition. Existing one-step physics-informed generative models must jointly control data fidelity and physical constraints without the iterative correction of multi-step samplers, making it difficult to coordinate indirect surrogate supervision with strong physics enforcement. PI-LSFM addresses this challenge by decomposing generation into a long flow map for global transport and a near-terminal short flow map, where closed-form data and physics potentials provide directly computable guidance targets instead of indirect regression surrogates. The short map guides the long map during training, yielding a single one-step generator that requires neither staged distillation nor inference-time correction. Across Darcy flow, Kolmogorov flow, dynamic stall, and topology optimization, PI-LSFM achieves a favorable trade-off among distributional fidelity, physical residuals, and inference efficiency while using only one function evaluation at inference. 1 Introduction Many problems in scientific machine learning are inherently distributional: under uncertain boundary conditions, perturbed parameters, incomplete observations, or intrinsic stochasticity, one seeks not a single deterministic solution, but a distribution of physically feasible ones. This makes generative modeling a natural framework for physical systems, as it can capture high-dimensional solution distributions while incorporating PDEs, conservation laws, and other physical constraints. Recent works have therefore introduced physics-informed diffusion and related generative frameworks to produce samples that are both statistically plausible and physically valid Shu et al. (2023) ; Huang et al. (2024) ; Jacobsen et al. (2025) . However, these methods typically rely on iterative multi-step generation and are often slow for practical use, which naturally motivates fast and ideally one-step physics-informed generation. The main difficulty, however, is not merely that one-step generation is harder to train, but that existing physics-informed diffusion methods rely on indirect supervision for both data and physics. On the data side, flow matching learns the data distribution through the surrogate regression objective ℒ data = 𝔼 ⁡ [ | u t θ ​ ( x t ) − u t ​ ( x t | x 1 ) | 2 ] \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{data}}=\mathbb{E}[|u_{t}^{\theta}(x_{t})-u_{t}(x_{t}|x_{1})|^{2}] , where the model is supervised by the conditional velocity u t ​ ( x t | x 1 ) u_{t}(x_{t}|x_{1}) because the true marginal velocity u t ​ ( x t ) u_{t}(x_{t}) is unavailable. On the physics side, directly applying a nonlinear residual to intermediate states causes a Jensen-type mismatch Bastek et al. (2024) ; existing methods therefore impose the residual on a reconstructed endpoint, ℒ phys = 𝔼 ⁡ [ | ℛ ⁡ ( x ^ 1 ​ ( x t ) ) | 2 ] \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{phys}}=\mathbb{E}[|\mathcal{R}(\hat{x}_{1}(x_{t}))|^{2}] , and use it to supervise intermediate states indirectly. This double indirectness makes distributional and physical objectives difficult to coordinate Baldan et al. (2026) . The issue is amplified in one-step methods such as MeanFlow Geng et al. (2025) and ShortCut Frans et al. (2025) . A long-range flow map ψ t → r \psi_{t\to r} is difficult to learn and, unlike an instantaneous velocity, lacks a consistent data-conditioned counterpart ψ t → r ( ⋅ | x 1 ) \psi_{t\to r}(\cdot|x_{1}) for surrogate supervision Li et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2026) . Moreover, one-step sampling removes the iterative correction available in multi-step methods Bastek et al. (2024) , requiring stronger physics enforcement during training. Thus, one-step physics-informed generation must couple a harder indirect distribution objective with a stronger physics objective, making training fragile. Even in endpoint-prediction methods such as sCM Lu & Song (2024) , where the residual can be applied directly to ψ t → 1 ​ ( x t ) \psi_{t\to 1}(x_{t}) , the data objective remains indirect. Chang et al. (2026) show that coupling strong physics constraints with indirect distribution objectives can lead to trivial solutions, severe mode collapse, and the need for two-stage distillation. Figure 1: PI-LSFM enables physics-informed one-step generation from scratch via long-short flow-map direct guidance, achieving multi-step-level performance on unconditional generation, conditional generation, and inverse design without increasing batch size or training steps, and without extra inference-time parameters or iterative correction. In this work, we study physics-informed one-step generation in flow-map-based frameworks and aim to enable stable training from scratch through direct data-distribution and physics-constraint objectives. This is difficult in existing methods: closed-form flow-matching solutions are typically too inefficient for practical training Bertrand et al. (2025) , while directly imposing physical constraints at intermediate states leads to Jensen’s gap. Our key observation is that both objectives can be imposed directly in the near-terminal data neighborhood, where they provide effective and correct guidance for learning the full flow map. This motivates a long-short flow-map approach, which decomposes one-step generation into a long flow map for global evolution and a near-terminal short flow map driven by computable closed-form solutions and physics potentials. As Δ ​ t → 0 \Delta t\to 0 , the short flow map shrinks away while providing direct data-distribution and physics-constraint guidance for learning the long flow map. This yields Long-Short Flow Maps with Direct Guidance (PI-LSFM), where data learning and physical validity are guided by near-terminal, directly computable targets rather than conditional-regression surrogates or reconstructed terminal states. A detailed discussion of related work is provided in Appendix A . Our contributions: (1) We propose a long-short flow-map framework that addresses indirect-objective instability by modeling the short flow map as dynamics jointly driven by data and physics potentials, enabling direct guidance from distributional and physical constraints for one-step generation. (2) We study the numerical design and computation of the short flow map, leading to a stable and efficient training procedure with improved distributional fidelity and physical consistency.
